question.:question/problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=-3.$ Given that the point $P(2,-3,3)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=6(x-1)$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $y=-3.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(2,-3).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(x,y)$ at $(2,-3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(2,-3) & =6(2-1)=6\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(2,-3) & ={f}_{x}(2,-3)(x-2) \\ z-3 & =6(x-2) \\ z-3 & =6x-12 \\ z & =6x-9\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,1,0)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
{\begin{aligned}y=-3 \\ z=6x-9\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $y=-3,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨0,1,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=6x-9$ (or $6x-z-9=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨6,0,-1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨0,1,0⟩\times ⟨6,0,-1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 6 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-i-6\,k \\  & =⟨-1,0,-6⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $⟨-1,0,-6⟩$ is parallel to the tangent line, then $-⟨-1,0,-6⟩=⟨1,0,6⟩$ is also parallel to it.

question.:question/problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=1.$ Given that the point $P(1,-1,2)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}={x}^{2}(2xy-1)$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $x=1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(1,-1).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ at $(1,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(1,-1) & =(1)^{2}(2(1)(-1)-1)=-3\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(1,-1) & ={f}_{y}(1,-1)(y+1) \\ z-2 & =-3(y+1) \\ z-2 & =-3y-3 \\ z & =-3y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,-1,2)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=1 \\ z=-3y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $x=1,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=-3y-1$ (or $-3y-z-1=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨0,-3,-1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,0,0⟩\times ⟨0,-3,-1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =j-3\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to $C$ at $P$ is $j-3\,k.$

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(-2,2) & ={f}_{y}(-2,2)(y-2) \\ z-3 & =2(y-2) \\ z & =2y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(-2,2,3)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=-2 \\ z=2y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $x=-2,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=2y-1$ (or $2y-z-1=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨0,2,-1⟩.$

$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(1,0) & ={f}_{y}(1,0)(y-0) \\ z-(-1) & =(-1)y \\ z & =-y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,0,-1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=1 \\ z=-y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $x=1,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=-y-1$ (or $y+z+1=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨0,1,1⟩.$

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=-2 \\ z=-y-5\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $x=-2,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=-y-5$ (or $y+z+5=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨0,1,1⟩.$

question.:question/problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=-1.$ Given that the point $P(-1,0,\frac{1}{2})$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=\frac{x(y-x)}{2x(y+1)}$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$

The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $x=-1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(-1,0).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ at $(-1,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(-1,0) & =\frac{(-1)(0-(-1))}{2(-1)(0+1)} \\  & =\frac{-1}{-2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(-1,0) & ={f}_{y}(-1,0)(y-0) \\ z-\frac{1}{2} & =\frac{1}{2}y \\ z & =\frac{1}{2}y+\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(-1,0,\frac{1}{2})$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=-1 \\ z=\frac{1}{2}y+\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $x=-1,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=\frac{1}{2}y+\frac{1}{2}$ (or $y-2z+1=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨0,1,-2⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,0,0⟩\times ⟨0,1,-2⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -2\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =2\,j+k \\  & =⟨0,2,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to $C$ at $P$ is $⟨0,2,1⟩.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(-2,2) & =9\left((-2)^{2}(2)+2(-2)-(2)\right) \\  & =9\left(8-4-2\right) \\  & =18\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(-2,2) & ={f}_{y}(-2,2)(y-(2)) \\ z-(3) & =(18)(y-(2)) \\ z & =18 y - 33\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\{x=-2 \\ z=18 y - 33\end{aligned}

- For the plane $z=18 y - 33$ (or $18 y - z - 33=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨0,18,-1⟩.$

The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $x=1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(1,0).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ at $(1,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(1,0) & =9\left(1\cdot {e}^{1\cdot 0}-2\operatorname{cos}⁡0\right) \\  & =9\left(1\cdot 1-2\cdot 1\right) \\  & =-9\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(1,0) & ={f}_{y}(1,0)(y-(0)) \\ z-(-1) & =(-9)(y-(0)) \\ z & =- 9 y - 1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,0,-1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{x=1 \\ z=- 9 y - 1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $x=1,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=- 9 y - 1$ (or $9 y + z + 1=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨0,9,1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,0,0⟩\times ⟨0,9,1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 9 & 1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =- j + 9 k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to $C$ at $P$ is $- j + 9 k.$

question.:question/problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=4.$ Given that the point $P(-2,4,0)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=(9)x$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $y=4.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(-2,4).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(x,y)$ at $(-2,4):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(-2,4) & =(9)(-2)=-18\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(-2,4) & ={f}_{x}(-2,4)(x-(-2)) \\ z-(0) & =(-18)(x-(-2)) \\ z-(0) & =- 18 x - 36 \\ z & =- 18 x - 36\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(-2,4,0)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{y=4 \\ z=- 18 x - 36\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $y=4,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨0,1,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=- 18 x - 36$ (or $- 18 x - z - 36=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨-18,0,-1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨0,1,0⟩\times ⟨-18,0,-1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -18 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =- i + 18 k \\  & =⟨-1,0,18⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $⟨-1,0,18⟩$ is parallel to the tangent line, then $-(⟨-1,0,18⟩)=⟨1,0,-18⟩$ is also parallel to it.

- For the plane $z=- 24 x - 97$ (or $- 24 x - z - 97=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨-24,0,-1⟩.$
